I am 63 years old and have been farming these lands in Quzhou for 40 years. I know every mu of my 10.1 mu farm like the back of my hand. My wife and I are the only ones working it now—our children have gone to the city—so I cannot take on more than we two can handle. But I also cannot afford to let land sit idle.

I will keep my **wheat-maize rotation on 7 mu** because it is reliable. Wheat feeds us and the maize brings cash. I plant **wheat in October** using improved seeds—about 30 jin per mu. Before sowing, I run the rotary tiller to break up the stubble and level the field. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer as basal and topdress with urea at green-up and jointing. I have learned over the years that about 15 kg of nitrogen, 7 kg of phosphorus, and 5 kg of potassium per mu gives me a good stand without wasting money. I will irrigate three times: once before winter to protect the seedlings, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. The wheat will need three pesticide sprays—herbicide after sowing, then fungicide and insecticide when the weather turns humid. I expect around 500 kg per mu if the spring rain cooperates.

Right after harvesting the wheat in early June, I sow **summer maize** on the same 7 mu. I use hybrid seed—Nongda or something similar—about 1.2 packages per mu. I do not till for maize; I plant directly into the wheat stubble. This saves me labor and fuel, and the maize does fine. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress with urea when the plants are knee-high. I give it 14 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. Maize needs less water than wheat, so two irrigations are enough—one at the big trumpet stage and one at filling. Three pesticide applications should handle the weeds and borers. If all goes well, I will get about 550 kg per mu.

The remaining **3.1 mu I keep in cotton**. Cotton is hard work—I am getting older and my back aches after pruning—but the price is usually better than maize, and I have grown it for decades. I rotary till in April and sow improved cotton seed, about 3 jin per mu. Cotton is hungry and thirsty, so I apply 12 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu, mostly as compound fertilizer. I irrigate twice, once at flowering and once at boll stage. The bollworm is my biggest enemy, so I spray pesticide 12 times through the season—better to spray early than lose the crop. I expect about 230 kg of seed cotton per mu.

This plan keeps my family fed, covers our costs, and does not require more labor than my wife and I can manage at our age.
